an0893.assistant:

The problem is the 11% repeat. For a coffee brand that number should scare you, because coffee is a consumable — people who like it should be reordering every few weeks. An 11% 90-day repeat means almost nobody comes back for a second bag. You're earning ₹500 once per customer and then they vanish, so your real LTV is basically just that first order. Scale ad spend now and all you do is buy more one-time strangers faster.

The single move: fix repeat before you add a rupee to ads. A consumable brand lives or dies on the second order — a simple reorder nudge on WhatsApp/email at day 20-25, or a subscribe-and-save, can move that 11% materially.

Caveat: 11% over one 30-day window of cohorts is directional, not gospel — pull the actual 90-day cohort for buyers from 3-4 months ago to confirm the leak is structural and not just young cohorts that haven't had time to reorder yet.

an0894.user: Need a gut check. Apparel label, doing about ₹25L a month over the last quarter. My problem is everyone keeps telling me my Amazon Ads ACoS is creeping up and I should fix the campaigns. an0894.assistant:

That's concentration risk, not an efficiency problem. The unit economics being fine is exactly what makes it dangerous: it feels safe, so you keep feeding the one channel. But the failure mode here isn't gradual. One Amazon algorithm change, a suspended ad account, a category CPM spike, or a policy strike, and ₹23.5L doesn't dip — it can halve overnight, and you have no second engine to catch it.

The lever: start a genuine second channel now, while it's a choice and not an emergency. Meta/Instagram for the brand, or your own D2C site with WhatsApp retention — something where you own the customer relationship, not Amazon. Even getting that 6% to 20-25% over two quarters changes your risk profile completely.

The honest caveat: I can't tell you which second channel pays back without seeing your margins off-Amazon and your category's CAC there — the unit economics that work inside Amazon's marketplace won't automatically hold when you're buying cold traffic yourself. But the diversification call stands regardless of which channel you pick.

an0896.user: Salon chain, running SEO/organic and pushing it hard. Last 30 days: 470K impressions, 5,297 clicks, so CTR's around 1.1%. CTR isn't your problem, so don't spend a week chasing it. 1.1% on broad organic reach is unremarkable — the real damage is one step further down. 5,297 clicks turned into 26 orders. That's a 0.49% conversion rate, and that's the number screaming.

Here's the mechanism: broad-match keywords are doing exactly what broad-match does — pulling in enormous volume of people who typed something loosely related and are browsing, comparing, or just curious. High impressions, decent clicks, and almost nobody with intent to actually book. You're buying tyre-kickers, not buyers. Lifting CTR would just bring more of the same low-intent crowd.

The lever: tighten intent. Cut the broad-match terms back to high-intent phrases ("[service] near me", "[service] booking [city]", branded), pile on negative keywords to kill the junk queries, and stop optimising for clicks entirely — optimise for bookings. A smaller, sharper traffic stream that converts at even 2-3% beats this fire-hose at 0.49%.

One caveat: 26 orders is a thin base to draw a hard line on, so confirm the pattern holds across a couple more weeks. But the direction is clear — the leak is intent, not the headline CTR.

an0897.user: Quick one — candle brand, selling via Meesho Ads. Why is my CTR low? It's sitting at 1.7%. Last 30 days I had 25,000 visits, 2,470 added to cart, 1,408 reached checkout, and 423 actually purchased. I keep thinking if I fix the creative and bump CTR the sales will follow.

Walk the funnel one more step and the real wound shows up: 1,408 reached checkout, but only 423 bought. That's a 30% checkout-to-purchase rate. The mechanism is friction at the final step, not acquisition: a shipping or handling charge that surprises them at checkout, a forced login or OTP loop, a clunky address form, or a missing/failing payment option (UPI or COD not showing). Your ad money is doing its job; the cart is where it dies.

The lever: instrument the checkout step and watch where the 985 lost people drop — then fix that one thing. Don't touch the creative.

Caveat: Meesho's own checkout flow limits how much you control versus a native site — so first confirm whether this drop is your storefront or the platform's checkout, because the fix differs.

an0898.user: New to managing this properly, so bear with me. We sell vertical SaaS for clinics, running Google Performance Max. an0898.assistant:

Here's the mechanism. Performance Max found your best, highest-intent pockets first and converted them cheaply — that's the ₹509 CAC and 2.9 ROAS at the start. There are only so many clinics actively looking for your product in a given window. Once you'd mopped up the warm demand, the extra ₹6.4L had nowhere efficient to go, so the algorithm bought colder, pricier reach. More budget into a finite pool = each next customer costs more. The drop isn't a mistake in your account; it's physics.

Still, sanity-check the floor: even at ROAS 2.0, ₹1,500 × 50% = ₹750 gross, minus ₹764 CAC, you're at roughly −₹14 per order. You've scaled right past breakeven, which is why this hurts.

The lever: stop pushing more budget into the same pool. Create new demand instead — new audiences, fresh creative angles, or a second channel — to widen the pool before you widen the spend.

Caveat: 8 weeks of Pmax includes a learning period after each budget jump, so give any change 2-3 weeks to settle before reading the new CAC.

an0899.user: Salon chain, YouTube ads. Pasting what I've got — this week vs last week, conversion rate dropped 11%. Got 85 conversions this week. I'm honestly ready to tear up the whole strategy and rebuild it. What's wrong?!
an0899.assistant:

This is exactly how founders wreck their own accounts: react to a noisy week, change everything, then the next week reverts and now you can't tell what your changes did. The whipsaw costs you more than the dip ever would.

What to actually do this week: nothing. Let it run untouched.

A real signal looks like one of two things — the same direction holding for 3-4 consecutive weeks, or a single-week swing big enough that it can't be coincidence at your volume (think a 30-40%+ drop, not 11%). Until you see that, treat this as weather, not climate. Check back in 3 weeks.
